common_name: Prince of Austria Tulip (Heirloom Fragrant Single Early Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fall after the soil has cooled; this 1860 Dutch heirloom is prized for its strong, sweet fragrance.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained soil in full sun in fall, setting them four to six inches deep. 'Prince of Austria' is a Single Early class tulip dating to 1860, valued by heirloom-bulb growers for its warm orange-scarlet blooms flushed with carmine and its unusually strong, sweet scent compared to most modern tulips. It opens early in the tulip season and tends to be a reliable perennializer in favorable sites. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: Royal General Bulb Growers' Association (KAVB) tulip classification

common_name: Clara Butt Tulip (Heirloom Salmon-Pink Darwin Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs five to six inches deep in fall; this 1889 Darwin-class heirloom was once among the most widely grown tulips in Europe.

directions: Set bulbs five to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in autumn. 'Clara Butt' is a Darwin-class tulip introduced in 1889 and named for the English opera singer, known for its soft salmon-pink, egg-shaped blooms on tall, sturdy stems. It flowers in mid-to-late spring and was for decades one of the most commercially grown tulips in the Netherlands before falling out of fashion, making it a favorite of heirloom-bulb specialists today. It combines well with other pastel-toned late tulips in mixed borders.
sources: Royal General Bulb Growers' Association (KAVB) tulip classification

common_name: Murillo Tulip (Heirloom Double Early Blush Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fall; this 1860 Double Early heirloom was once the most widely planted double tulip in cultivation.

directions: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun during fall. 'Murillo' is a Double Early class tulip dating to 1860, bearing fully double, peony-like blooms in a soft blush-white that sometimes shows faint pink feathering. It opens early in the season and its heavy flowers benefit from a somewhat sheltered spot out of strong wind. Historically it was propagated so widely that it became a parent or namesake for several later double-tulip sports.
sources: Royal General Bulb Growers' Association (KAVB) tulip classification

common_name: General de Wet Tulip (Heirloom Fragrant Flame-Orange Single Early Tulip)

planting.note: Plant bulbs four to six inches deep in fall; this 1904 Single Early heirloom is noted for its vivid color and carries real fragrance.

directions: Set bulbs four to six inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in autumn. 'General de Wet' is a Single Early class tulip introduced in 1904, with glowing orange petals flamed and feathered scarlet-red, and a sweet fragrance stronger than most tulips of its era. It opens early and holds its vivid coloring well even in cool spring weather. This heirloom is best sited where its fragrance can be appreciated near a path or doorway.
sources: Royal General Bulb Growers' Association (KAVB) tulip classification

common_name: Duc van Tol Red and Yellow Tulip (Ancient Dwarf Early Tulip)
scientific_name: Tulipa 'Duc van Tol Red and Yellow'

planting.note: Plant bulbs three to five inches deep in fall; the Duc van Tol strain is among the oldest tulip lines still grown, dating to the late 1500s.

directions: Plant bulbs three to five inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun during fall. Duc van Tol tulips are a dwarf strain tracing back to the late sixteenth century, long grown by Dutch nurserymen for forcing because they bloom earlier than almost any other tulip. This red-and-yellow form carries compact, rounded blooms of red petals edged in gold on short, sturdy stems close to the ground. Its small size suits rock gardens, container displays, and the front of a border where taller tulips would overshadow it.
sources: Royal General Bulb Growers' Association (KAVB) tulip classification

planting.note: Plant bulbs five to six inches deep in fall; this ancient double poeticus narcissus is one of the latest daffodils to bloom each spring.

directions: Set bulbs five to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in a sunny to lightly shaded spot in fall. This heirloom double form of the poet's narcissus has been grown in European gardens for centuries, producing fully double, pure white rosette-like blooms with faint creamy-yellow fragments at the center and an intense, sweet perfume. It is among the last narcissus to flower each spring, extending the daffodil season into late spring. Left undisturbed, it naturalizes readily in grass and old garden beds.
